results.corrected_extracted: Two groups of people who all used several drugs, recruited at private parties or a nightclub and aged 18 to 29: 20 who had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before testing, and 19 who had little or no previous ketamine use and had not taken it that evening. Both groups were tested on the night (day 0) in a small quiet room away from the music and again 3 days later (day 3) in their homes, with the same 25–35-minute battery in the same order; 7 more people tested once were not retested and 2 were discarded for taking drugs on the day of the second session. Story (prose) recall was scored in idea units, maximum 21, and the speed of comprehension test asked people to judge as many of 100 sentences as they could in 2 minutes. The self-ratings were an adapted dissociative states scale, a state schizotypal symptom questionnaire built for the study, a mood scale, 14 symptom ratings anchored at no symptom and severe symptom, and an anxiety and depression questionnaire rated for the last two days; no measure asked why people took ketamine or whether they enjoyed it.

results.corrected_extracted: A second narrative review, written for a UK scientific committee, describes ketamine as a non-competitive antagonist at the NMDA receptor, one of three glutamate receptors, central to learning and memory; it adds that ketamine blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, may strengthen GABA inhibition, induces dopamine release and acts as a weak opioid agonist, and that the two mirror-image forms differ in their affinity at the NMDA receptor while having similar pharmacokinetic profiles. Several of these statements carry no reference, and where the review cites imaging studies for striatal dopamine release two of the three papers are, by their titles, not dopamine-binding studies.
